desc:
A stage is a grid with one row per scene and one column per spotlight position. points[r][c] is the score earned when scene r is lit from position c.

You must choose exactly one position for every scene. Moving the spotlight between two consecutive scenes from position a to position b costs |a - b| points. The total is the sum of the chosen scores minus the sum of all moving costs. Return the largest total you can obtain.
hints: Choosing the best cell in every row greedily ignores the penalty. Let the decision for a row depend on where the previous row ended.

Let f[r][c] be the best total of scenes 0..r if scene r uses position c. Then f[r][c] = points[r][c] + max over b of (f[r-1][b] - |b - c|). Evaluating that maximum for every c directly costs O(n2) per row.

Split the absolute value. For positions b ≤ c you need max(f[r-1][b] + b) - c, and for b ≥ c you need max(f[r-1][b] - b) + c. Both are running maxima: one left-to-right sweep and one right-to-left sweep per row, i.e. left[c] = max(prev[c], left[c-1] - 1) and the mirrored right[c].
editorial: The recurrence f[r][c] = points[r][c] + max over b of (f[r-1][b] - |b - c|) is correct but takes O(m · n2) time. The maximum can be computed for all c at once because the penalty is linear in the distance: the best previous value seen from the left, discounted by one for every column travelled, is left[c] = max(prev[c], left[c-1] - 1), and symmetrically right[c] = max(prev[c], right[c+1] - 1).

Then f[r][c] = points[r][c] + max(left[c], right[c]). Staying in the same column corresponds to the term prev[c] that both sweeps include. The answer is the maximum of the last row. The total time is O(m · n) and the space O(n). The result is at most 60 · 100,000, well within 32-bit range.
